sentences.text: Kank was a medium-sized unenlagiid dinosaur whose bones are comparable in size to those of Neuquenraptor, which is estimated to have weighed about 27 kg.
Its teeth were small and curved toward the tip, lacking any serrations.
The teeth in the upper jaw were straight and showed no inward curvature on the tongue side.
These teeth displayed flutes that run from tip to base around side grooves, but no serrated ridges were present.
Lower-jaw teeth possessed ridges on the front side that were confined to the upper third of the crown, a condition similar to that seen in the unenlagiid dinosaur Austroraptor.
Like the unenlagiid dinosaur Buitreraptor, the upper-jaw teeth were laterally compressed in cross-section.
Kank is the first unenlagiid dinosaur recorded from the Chorrillo Formation.
The genus name honors the "elder Rhea" of Aonikenk mythology, who is said to have created the Southern Cross constellation.
The species epithet australis translates as "from the south" in Latin, referring to its southern discovery site.
Additional material that may belong to Kank includes a dorsal vertebra, a toe claw, and isolated teeth.
The genus Kank was uncovered in the Chorrillo Formation of southwestern Patagonia, Argentina.
Its holotype consists of a single vertebra, catalogued as specimen MPM-PV-23106-A.
Three toe bones and five teeth were recovered together with the holotype vertebra.
Kank was formally described by Motta and colleagues, with Matías J. Motta, Alexis M. Aranciaga Rolando, and eleven other researchers as authors.
The type locality for the species is the Chorrillo Formation.
It is currently regarded as a valid taxon and represents both a new genus and a new species.
Only fragmentary fossils are known, limiting detailed knowledge of its biology.
Kank belongs to the unenlagiid theropod group.
Its parent family is Unenlagiidae.
It is placed within the class Reptilia.
Kank lived during the Late Cretaceous Maastrichtian age.
Its age range is dated between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
It inhabited a wetland environment that included both terrestrial and freshwater areas, as indicated by associated fish fossils.
